items.title: Vehicle plows into pedestrians in Los Angeles, killing three
items.content_html:
LOS ANGELES, Nov 10 (Reuters) - An SUV plowed into a group of pedestrians in the North Hollywood district of Los Angeles on Tuesday, killing at least three and critically injuring three more, authorities said.

No official details were immediately available about the incident, which happened shortly before 6 p.m. PST (0200 GMT). A police spokesperson said investigators had yet to determine if the crash was accidental or deliberate.

"We need to understand exactly what happened and what led to this tragedy," Los Angeles County Supervisor Kathryn Barger said in a statement. "I will be closely following the investigation and seeking additional information as the facts emerge."

Three people hit by the vehicle were declared dead at the scene, while two pedestrians and the driver of the vehicle, were taken to hospitals, the Los Angeles police and fire departments said.

Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass said the SUV drove onto a sidewalk and struck a group of street vendors and pedestrians, adding that first responders were on the scene and that her office was working closely with city departments.

"I'm heartbroken for the families of everyone impacted," she added on X, promising updates as more information came in.

Television station KCAL-TV, a CBS News affiliate, said a car crashed into a food stand near a bus stop along Lankershim Boulevard a major road through the busy NoHo commercial and arts district in the city's San Fernando Valley.

A small white partially crumpled SUV appeared to have run up on to the sidewalk under a blue canopy to hit the side of a mass-transit shelter structure, aerial news images from KCAL showed.

Reporting by Steve Gorman in Los Angeles and Jasper Ward and Kanishka Singh in Washington and Rhea Rose Abraham in Bengaluru; Editing by Michelle Nichols, Lincoln Feast and Clarence Fernandez

items.title: Baby boy found alive in US after believed buried for 24 hours, police say
items.content_html:
Nov 10 (Reuters) - An 11-month-old boy was found alive in South Carolina on Tuesday after he was believed to have been buried for about 24 hours, the Lexington County Sheriff's Department said.

The infant, Koah Sharpe, was found wrapped in a towel in a dog crate, shallowly buried in woods, according to the department.

"Certainly God is good. Just a few moments ago, we found little Koah, 11 months old, buried alive, clinging to life, crying — the most joyful sound you ever heard of a crying baby," Lexington County Sheriff Jay Koon said during a news conference.

Koon said the infant's father, Michael Comer, was arrested on Monday night on burglary and resisting arrest. The department is working with the solicitor's office to determine additional charges, he said.

Koah went missing on Monday after being left in his father's care at his mother's home while she ran an errand, Koon said. The boy was reported missing and authorities began a widespread search, according to the sheriff.

Koah was found after a search party discovered "freshly disturbed" dirt in the woods about 50 yards from Comer's father's house, Koon said.

The infant is currently at the hospital and will "hopefully" recover, the sheriff said.

Reporting by Jasper Ward in Washington; editing by Michelle Nichols

items.title: Kennedy family tries to stop Trump's Washington arch
items.content_html:
Nov 10 (Reuters) - Several members of the Kennedy family, one of America's most famous political dynasties, filed on Tuesday to join a court case aimed at stopping President Donald Trump from building a proposed triumphal arch in Washington, saying it would obstruct views and cast shadows over their relatives' grave sites.

The 250-foot (76-meter) arch, shown in a rendering to include a flame held by a 60-foot gold winged female figure and flanked by gold flying eagles, would be situated across the Potomac River from the Lincoln Memorial on a highway roundabout near the entrance to the Arlington National Cemetery.

A judge has already issued a temporary order blocking construction through November 19 as she considers whether to issue a preliminary injunction.

The arch "will permanently cast shadows over and damage historically significant sight lines to the existing grave sites and memorials established in the Kennedy family's honor at Arlington National Cemetery, as well as to the memorials of hundreds of thousands of fallen American heroes," the filing said.

The Kennedy family is one of the most prolific political dynasties in US history, notably including former President John F. Kennedy. Trump's health secretary is Robert F. Kennedy Jr., nephew to the assassinated former president.

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Reuters.

The Trump administration contends Congress approved the arch more than 100 years ago when it also authorized construction of a bridge across the Potomac River. It has said that the arch would honor veterans.

Numerous Democrats in Congress have vowed to block construction once they take control in January, after winning November's midterm elections.

Additional reporting by David Shepardson; editing by Michelle Nichols

items.title: US House votes to derail impeachment of Defense Secretary Hegseth
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 10 (Reuters) - Republicans in the US House of Representatives banded together on Tuesday to derail an effort to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

The chamber voted 211 to 204 in favor of a motion to refer the impeachment charges to the Republican-led House Judiciary Committee, effectively stopping the effort to impeach Hegseth sponsored by Kentucky Republican Representative Thomas Massie.

Massie was the only Republican who voted against the motion.

Reporting by Patricia Zengerle; Editing by Chris Reese

items.title: US consumer prices rise briskly for third straight month
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 10 (Reuters) - US consumer prices increased more than expected in October amid higher costs for food and accommodation, cementing expectations that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates next month.

The Consumer Price Index report from the Labor Department on Tuesday also showed a strong buildup of underlying inflation pressures for a third straight month. It followed data last week showing the labor market regained momentum in October.

Inflation is being driven by the US-Israeli war with Iran, which has boosted oil prices, the Trump administration's import tariffs, resilient consumer spending and aggressive business investment in artificial intelligence technology.

The rising cost of living contributed to the heavy losses suffered by President Donald Trump's Republican Party in the midterm elections last week.

Fed Governor Christopher Waller said on Tuesday the US central bank should raise rates next month, adding that "a stronger policy move may be needed." Waller also raised the prospect of an aggressive 50-basis-point hike.

"The Fed seems to be falling behind the curve on inflation, and the October hold is looking like a policy mistake," said Stephen Juneau, an economist at Bank of America Securities. "We see a rising risk that the Fed will have to hike again in January, rather than March."

The CPI increased 0.4% last month after advancing 0.6% in September, the department's Bureau of Labor Statistics said. It was the third consecutive month of gains of 0.4% or more. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast the CPI would climb 0.3% over the month. The BLS did not publish year-over-year inflation readings because last year's federal government shutdown prevented the collection of consumer price data in October 2025, leaving no comparison base.

Some economists used the average index for September and November 2025 to estimate the year-over-year rate of change for the October CPI. Others used interpolated levels from independent sources. Their estimates for the October year-over-year CPI ranged from a gain of 3.9% to 4.0%. Annual consumer inflation was 3.7% in September.

Shelter, which includes rents and hotel and motel rooms, accounted for more than 30% of the monthly increase in the CPI. Shelter costs rose 0.3% after climbing 0.4% in September.

Food prices surged 0.5% after barely rising in the prior three months. Grocery store prices climbed 0.4%, boosted by a 0.9% jump in the cost of beef. Egg prices rose 0.6%, while fruits and vegetables were 0.6% more expensive. Prices for dairy products increased 0.6%. The cost of snacks surged 1.0%.

Rising prices at the supermarket could be an early sign that high diesel prices are filtering through to consumers. The cost of eating out also increased last month, with prices of food away from home rising 0.5% after a 0.2% gain in September. The cost of full-service meals jumped 0.7%.

"This may finally be the beginning of a pass-through of higher transportation costs to grocery prices," said Stephen Stanley, chief US economist at Santander US Capital Markets. "If this is indeed happening, it could be a feature across a broad array of goods categories."

Gasoline prices climbed 1.0% after soaring 9.1% in September. Consumers also paid more for electricity. Although diesel prices have eased off all-time highs, they remain on an upward trend, rising 2.7% in October after increasing 11.9% in September.

Consumers could get some relief at the pump, with oil prices down at least 10% so far this month, but the pressure is unlikely to ease elsewhere, economists warned.

Inflation-adjusted average weekly earnings fell again in October.

MORE RATE HIKES ANTICIPATED

The so-called core CPI, which excludes volatile food and energy items, increased 0.3% in October for the third straight month. The so-called core CPI was forecast to have climbed 0.2% in October. Economists estimated that year-over-year core CPI inflation gained 2.8% in October. Annual core CPI inflation rose 2.6% in September.

Financial markets are pricing in a roughly 89% chance of a 25-basis-point rate hike next month, and expect another increase in March, CME Group's FedWatch tool showed. The Fed left its benchmark overnight interest rate in the 3.75%-4.00% range last month. Economists said only a substantial selloff in equity markets or widening credit spreads would prevent the Fed from tightening monetary policy in December.

Stocks on Wall Street were trading lower. They slumped last week after the Democrats' sweeping victory fanned fears that new regulations could dent the durability of the AI trade, but rallied on Monday as oil prices fell. The dollar gained against a basket of currencies. US Treasury yields were mostly higher.

Underlying inflation last month was driven by a 0.3% rise in owners' equivalent rent, a measure of the amount homeowners would pay to rent or earn from renting their property. Prices for hotel and motel rooms rose 0.6%. Airline fares increased 0.4%. The cost of recreation services climbed 0.9%, while that of motor vehicle insurance advanced 0.7%.

Doctor visits and hospital services also cost more. But the price of health insurance dropped 1.8%. The BLS updated the data used to calculate this component. Overall services prices excluding energy increased 0.3% after rising 0.4% in September.

Tariff effects were also evident in October. Prices of household furnishings and supplies rebounded 0.7% and the cost of toys increased 1.8%. There were more price gains for computers and peripherals, reflecting the AI spending boom. Prices for smartphones rose a record 1.4%.

There were also increases in the prices of new vehicles and medication. But used car and truck prices dropped 1.2%. Core goods prices increased 0.2% after climbing 0.3% in September.

The missing data from last year have no impact on the calculation of the Personal Consumption Expenditures Price Index readings that the Fed tracks to gauge progress toward its inflation target.

Based on last month's data, economists estimated that core PCE inflation rose 0.4% after advancing 0.3% in September. In the 12 months through October, core PCE inflation is projected to have increased 3.3% after gaining 3.1% in the 12 months through September. These estimates could be impacted by producer price data for October that is due to be released on Friday.

"Inflation isn't dead; it is very much alive and the cost-of-living crisis rages on," said Christopher Rupkey, chief economist at FWDBONDS.

items.title: US traffic deaths fall in first half of 2026, lowest rate since 2014
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 10 (Reuters) - US traffic deaths fell in the first half of this year to the lowest rate since 2014, the government said on Tuesday, retreating from a spike during the 2020 COVID pandemic and several years in which road deaths remained elevated.

This year is on pace to be the fifth straight year of declines, according to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, which said traffic deaths dropped 2.5% to 16,750 in the first half of the year. It was the lowest number since 2015 and down from 17,175 in the same period last year.

The fatality rate fell to 1.02 fatalities per 100 million vehicle miles traveled and the number of deaths fell to the lowest number since 2015.

Full-year traffic deaths for 2025 fell to the lowest number since 2019 and the fatality rate fell to 1.10 fatalities per 100 million vehicle miles traveled, the second-lowest yearly figure in US history, NHTSA said.

Deaths fell 5% in the first three months of 2026 but just 0.2% in the second three months.

One area of concern remains bicyclist deaths, which rose 4% to 1,148 last year. In 2023, bicyclist deaths hit their highest figure in more than four decades.

US traffic deaths jumped 10.8% in 2021 to 43,230, the most in a single year since 2005.

As US roads became less crowded during the pandemic, some motorists perceived police as less likely to issue tickets, experts said, resulting in riskier driving. Some drivers were also more likely to drive while being impaired by alcohol or drugs consumed at home during the pandemic.

The US fatality rate rose much higher than for other developed nations during the pandemic.

A 2023 NHTSA study found crashes directly cost taxpayers $30 billion, and society as a whole $340 billion. When quality-of-life valuations were included, the total cost to society ran to $1.37 trillion.

items.title: Most Americans want new Democratic Congress to end Trump's Iran war, Reuters/Ipsos poll finds
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 10 (Reuters) - Majorities of Americans want the newly elected Democratic-majority US Congress to act to end the war with Iran and to repeal tariffs put in place by President Donald Trump, signaling demand for quick action to address the high cost of living, a new Reuters/Ipsos poll found.

The four-day poll, completed on Monday, showed 71% of Americans -- including 93% of Democrats and 51% of Republicans -- want US Congress to pass legislation ending the conflict with Iran that Trump launched alongside US ally Israel in February.

Democrats won their largest majorities in the Senate and House of Representatives since at least 2008 in last week's midterm elections, in a sharp rebuke to Trump's Republicans over high costs and a deeply unpopular war. Democrats will take power when the new Congress is sworn in on January 3.

A smaller but still-significant share of respondents -- 62% -- said they would support an effort to repeal tariffs on imports put in place by the Trump administration.

The war with Iran has pushed fuel prices sharply higher, adding to inflation already stoked by the new taxes Trump slapped on hundreds of imported goods. Trump has defended the war as necessary to prevent Iran from acquiring a nuclear weapon. The tariffs, he has said, will boost American industry by protecting it from cheap imports.

Democratic Party leaders have vowed to address cost of living concerns, and say they will try to force an end to the US war with Iran. Many in the party have also vowed to end Trump's tariffs.

DESIRE FOR BIPARTISANSHIP

Large majorities of people in both political parties said it was important for Trump to make an effort to work with Democrats and for Democratic leaders in the new Congress to try to work with the president.

Nine in 10 respondents said cost of living issues should be a focus for the Congress during its first 100 days. Smaller shares wanted a focus on issues like artificial intelligence regulation, immigration reform and climate change.

OPPOSITION TO IMPEACHMENT

But many Americans appear concerned Democrats will use their new power to launch legal proceedings against Trump. Some 42% of poll respondents said it would be "bad for the country" if the new Congress tried to impeach Trump, compared with 33% who said it would be good for the country. The rest weren't sure or didn't answer the question.

Congressional Democrats are divided on how to bring down healthcare costs, and also disagree on how aggressively to target Trump, including whether to impeach the president or members of his cabinet. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth is expected to face a House impeachment vote this week, following a move by a Republican lawmaker.

While Trump said after the elections he would "probably" get along with Democrats, he also promoted Stephen Miller, a polarizing aide who has called the Democratic Party a domestic extremist group, to be his new White House chief of staff.

While the poll showed Trump's approval rating near the lowest level of his political career, at 32%, it also showed Democrats were not particularly popular either.

Some 45% of Americans had a favorable view of Democrats, while 51% had an unfavorable view. Some 35% had a favorable view of Republicans and 60% viewed them unfavorably.

Asked which party had a better approach to regulating artificial intelligence, which could be an important issue for Congress in the coming months, 28% picked Democrats and 20% picked Republicans while the rest said they weren't sure or that neither was better.

The Reuters/Ipsos poll, which was conducted online and nationwide, gathered responses from 1,705 US adults and had a margin of error of about 2 percentage points.

Reporting by Jason Lange in Washington; editing by Scott Malone and Deepa Babington

items.title: India, US continuing talks to finalise first tranche of trade deal, official says
items.content_html:
Nov 10 (Reuters) - India is continuing talks with the US to finalise the first tranche of a bilateral trade deal, and US officials visited the country earlier this month for discussions, an Indian official told reporters on Tuesday.

Discussions earlier this month centred on customs and trade facilitation issues, the official added.

The comments come after US President Donald Trump's Republican Party suffered heavy losses in the November 3 midterm elections, losing control of both chambers of the US Congress.

With some races still undecided, Democrats scored their biggest victory in the House of Representatives since at least 2008 while flipping Senate seats in traditionally conservative states including Kansas, South Carolina and Texas.

Reporting by Shivangi Acharya in New Delhi. Writing by Kanjyik Ghosh in Barcelona. Editing by Mark Potter

items.title: Trump administration moves to cut food stamps for 6.3 million people
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 10 (Reuters) - The Trump administration on Tuesday moved to cut millions more Americans from the nation's largest food assistance program, even as enrollment continues to fall from other administration cuts.

A proposed rule issued by the US Department of Agriculture would curb automatic eligibility for Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program benefits, also known as food stamps, for households receiving cash aid under the Temporary Assistance for Needy Families Program.

Currently, households receiving TANF benefits qualify for SNAP without needing to meet federal income thresholds. TANF eligibility varies by state but is generally 130% to 200% of the federal poverty level. SNAP eligibility is generally 130% of the federal poverty level.

Under the USDA's proposed change, nearly 18% of SNAP recipients, or about 6.3 million people, would lose benefits, according to an agency analysis included in the proposed rule.

The changes would make SNAP eligibility more standardized and "preserve benefits for the truly needy," the rule said.

More than 5.5 million people have already lost SNAP benefits since President Donald Trump enacted cuts to the program in his July 2025 tax law, bringing enrollment to about 36 million people, according to USDA data.

The enrollment decline is partly due to struggles by states to implement administrative changes to the program and also to absorb significant new costs from Trump's law.

Because SNAP enrollment also confers eligibility for other food aid programs, the USDA estimates that 1.8 million children would also lose eligibility for free school lunch under its proposed rule.

Democratic Representative Angie Craig of Minnesota, ranking member of the House Agriculture Committee, in a statement called the rule "heartless and cruel."

"The proposed rule would make it harder to meet basic needs and roll back efforts to streamline federal programs," she said.

The public will have 30 days to comment on the proposed rule.

Reporting by Leah Douglas in Washington; Editing by Bill Berkrot

items.title: What are the impeachment articles facing Pete Hegseth?
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, November 10 - Republican US Representative Thomas Massie introduced eight articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, related to the war in Iran, President Donald Trump's actions in Venezuela and even some administration actions in Washington.

Hegseth has denied wrongdoing, and Trump has criticized Massie and pledged to stand by his secretary of defense.

Here are the eight "high crimes and misdemeanors" in the unusual Republican-led impeachment effort against a Republican official.

IRAN

Three of the charges are related to the conflict in Iran. Hegseth is accused of directing, authorizing and sustaining military actions against Iran beyond a 60-day limit without a formal declaration of war or authorization for the use of military force (AUMF) by Congress.

A fourth Iran-related charge accuses Hegseth of ignoring laws requiring that US forces minimize civilian casualties, related to a strike on a girls school in Minab on February 28, the first day of the conflict, that killed scores of children.

VENEZUELA

Two charges are related to Venezuela, whose president, Nicolas Maduro, was removed by US forces in January 2026.

Hegseth is accused of directing the kidnapping of a sovereign foreign leader and authorizing extrajudicial lethal strikes in the Caribbean and Pacific that have resulted in more than 220 deaths.

YEMEN

Hegseth is accused of directing and executing unlawful military strikes and operations in Yemen, specifically "Operation Rough Rider," a 2025 US and British air and naval campaign against Iran-aligned Houthi fighters.

FREE SPEECH

Hegseth is accused of retaliating against Democratic Senator Mark Kelly of Arizona, despite legal protection of his speech.

Last year, Hegseth sought to prosecute Kelly and demote him from his retired Navy captain rank after he and five other Democrats in Congress with backgrounds in the military and intelligence urged US troops to refuse illegal orders.

Reporting by Patricia Zengerle
Editing by Nick Zieminski

items.title: Thune, Jordan emerge as Republican minority leaders for next US Congress
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 10 (Reuters) - Republicans chose US Senate Majority Leader John Thune and House Judiciary Committee Chairman Jim Jordan on Tuesday to lead them against a Democratic-controlled Congress that will take power in January for the final two years of Donald Trump's presidency.

A week after Republicans lost their majority in a stinging midterm election defeat, Senate Republicans chose Thune by acclamation at a closed-door meeting for the task of trying to thwart Democratic initiatives that do not meet with their approval, including by wielding the Senate filibuster.

"We're not going to be running this place next year," Thune told reporters. "But you can be assured we will be very, very active in asserting conservative priorities in all of the legislating ... that goes on here."

Jordan's election as House minority leader elevates a combative Trump ally to the forefront of the party's fight to defend the US president's agenda in the lower chamber. Jordan defeated House Majority Leader Steve Scalise in a secret ballot. House Speaker Mike Johnson opted not to stand for the leadership position.

The House and Senate leadership elections will help to determine what role Republicans intend to play as the minority party in Congress during the final two years of Trump's presidency.

Democrats will need Republican support to move major initiatives in the 100-member Senate, where the filibuster rule requires 60 votes for most legislation. Their majorities in both chambers also fall well short of the two-thirds of votes needed to override presidential vetoes.

Thune, 65, a South Dakota Republican known for his consensus-building leadership style, is respected by Republicans and Democrats alike. But he has run afoul of Trump's MAGA supporters who say he did not move aggressively enough to enact Trump's policies on immigration and election reform.

After the midterm elections, Thune vowed that Republicans would work with Trump to block "Democrat extremism" and work against any attempt by Democrats to unwind Republican achievements, including border security and judicial appointments.

Jordan, 62, was first elected in 2006 to represent a deeply conservative rural district in northern Ohio and was a founder of the House Freedom Caucus, a group that former Republican House Speaker John Boehner labeled "legislative terrorists."

Before entering politics, Jordan honed his pugilistic style during a career as a high school and university champion wrestler, and later as a wrestling coach at Ohio State University.

That past threatened his political career in 2018 when former students accused him of turning a blind eye to rampant sexual abuse of college wrestlers by the wrestling team's doctor, when Jordan was an assistant coach.

Jordan denied all allegations, and a university investigation found no hard evidence that he knew of the abuse. But former wrestlers said the doctor's abuse was well-known and the report itself found that students had complained about the doctor's voyeurism in front of coaching staff.

Jordan has often referred to his wrestling background in terms of his reputation as a fighter in Congress.

He is known for his aggressive style of questioning in committee hearings.

"I look at it like a wrestling match," Jordan told the New York Times in an April 2023 interview, explaining how he prepares for hearings. "I'm going to try to get as ready as I can. You can't just wing it."

Reporting by David Morgan; Editing by Michael Learmonth, Alistair Bell and Howard Goller

items.title: US sues Lyft, alleges discrimination against disabled riders
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 9 (Reuters) - The US Justice Department sued Lyft (LYFT.O) on Monday, alleging the ride-hailing services provider discriminated against passengers with disabilities, including those who use service animals and mobility devices such as stowable wheelchairs.

The lawsuit seeks $53 million for individuals with disabilities whom Lyft allegedly discriminated against, and who have submitted complaints to Lyft or the Department of Justice, the DOJ said in a statement.

Lyft said it disagreed with the allegations made in the Justice Department lawsuit that was filed in the US District Court for the Northern District of California.

The lawsuit alleges Lyft violated Title III of the Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990, which prohibits private transportation companies from discriminating based on disability.

The lawsuit seeks a court order to force Lyft to stop the alleged discrimination, to modify its policies to comply with the Americans with Disabilities Act, and to train its staff and drivers on the law, the Justice Department said.

The Justice Department alleged that Lyft and its drivers routinely refuse service to individuals with disabilities and refuse to reasonably modify Lyft's policies and practices to avoid such discrimination.

"We have long-standing policies requiring drivers to accommodate riders who travel with service animals or use foldable mobility devices, and drivers who violate these policies face serious consequences, including permanent deactivation," Lyft said in a statement responding to the lawsuit.

Lyft also said it has cooperated with the DOJ during its review.

Last year, the US government sued Uber (UBER.N), accusing the ride-sharing company of violating the same federal law by discriminating against passengers with disabilities.

That lawsuit sought $125 million for individuals subjected to the alleged discrimination and who previously submitted complaints to Uber or the Justice Department.

Uber had said it disagreed with all of the allegations, and was committed to expanding access and improving the experience of riders with disabilities.

items.title: Trump sets off bedlam in White House briefing room with UFC chief Dana White
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 9 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump set off a scramble in the White House press briefing room on Monday with ‌an appearance so sudden that aides had no time to place the presidential seal on the podium.

The cause of the sudden bedlam? Trump was eager to show off UFC CEO Dana White, a close friend more comfortable with watching fighters bash each other in the Octagon ​than mixing it up with reporters.

After heavy Republican losses in the midterm elections less than a week ago, ​Trump announced on Saturday that he had offered the White House press secretary job to White. ⁠Trump said on Sunday he was just teasing, but White came to the White House anyway to see the ​president.

"Everyone please take a seat in the briefing room RIGHT NOW," was a press assistant's urgent instruction for reporters over ​the loudspeaker.

The announcement set off a stampede among the press corps with TV technicians plugging in cables and setting up microphones. The spot on the podium where the presidential seal would normally hang was left vacant.

Appearing alongside White, Trump declared that White could be press secretary ​if he "would only take the job."

Trump has been searching for a press secretary since Karoline Leavitt left in August and ​her replacement, Katie Zacharia, was fired last month after a week.

"Dana is really very unique. The only problem is he'll talk for ‌a little ⁠while and then he's going to beat the hell out of you," Trump joked.

Trump announced that a UFC fight this weekend at Madison Square Garden will feature "the two greatest women fighters of all time."

"How would I do against one of them?" Trump asked White. "Would I do well?"

"I don't think so," White said.

White, who organized a series of UFC bouts on ​the White House grounds in ​June, made clear he had ⁠no desire to tussle with reporters.

"I have zero political aspirations," said White, while nonetheless taking a few questions.

In his first four years in office, Trump was a regular presence in ​the White House briefing room but now, nearly halfway through his second term, he ​takes questions in ⁠other places. He has talked about moving the press corps out of the West Wing to a "less obnoxious location."

But there was no talk of that on Monday. After Trump took questions on Iran, Ukraine, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang ⁠and other ​topics, he turned back to White.

"Would you like to be press secretary ​of the United States of America?" said Trump. "Would you like that, or do you just want to stay with that ridiculous UFC?"

"Thanks for the offer, ​sir," said White. "I do not want to be in politics."

Reporting by Steve Holland; Editing by Caitlin Webber and Stephen Coates

items.title: Trump approval holds at 32%, near lowest of his career, Reuters Ipsos poll finds
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 9 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump's approval rating held near the lowest level of his political career, depressed by national concerns over rising prices that tanked his Republican Party in last week's midterm elections, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll completed on Monday.

Some 32% of Americans approve of Trump's performance in the White House, unchanged from two prior Reuters/Ipsos polls conducted between late October and early November. It was one percentage point higher than his 31% rating in a Reuters/Ipsos poll in mid-October, the lowest of his career in politics.

Trump's Republican Party suffered a staggering defeat in the November 3 midterm elections, losing control of both chambers of the US Congress. With some races still undecided, Democrats scored their biggest victory in the House of Representatives since at least 2008 while flipping Senate seats in traditionally conservative states including Kansas, South Carolina and Texas.

The poll showed just 21% of Americans giving Trump a thumbs-up on his management of the cost of living. The war launched by the president on Iran in February has raised fuel prices sharply and weighed on household finances. Trump's low rating on the issue has also hurt his allies in Congress.

Trump's approval rating on immigration policy, at 38%, remains considerably higher than the 25% rating Americans give his economic stewardship.

Some 81% of Republicans in the poll supported Trump's immigration approach, compared with 50% who did so on the cost of living. Trump has aggressively ramped up deportations of immigrants since he returned to the White House in January 2025 and last week promoted Stephen Miller, a key architect of those policies, to be the new White House chief of staff.

The Reuters/Ipsos poll, which was conducted online nationwide November 6 to 9, gathered responses from 1,705 US adults and had a margin of error of about 2 percentage points.

Reporting by Jason Lange; editing by Scott Malone and Cynthia Osterman

items.title: Two arrested near White House in separate incidents, Secret Service says
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 9 (Reuters) - The U.S. Secret Service arrested two people near the White House on Monday after one person drove a car onto the sidewalk and another jumped a barricade at Lafayette Park in front of the presidential compound.

President Donald Trump was at home during the incidents. The White House was placed on lockdown briefly and roads around the park closed.

A car crashed into the sidewalk that surrounds Lafayette Park just before 10 a.m., a Secret Service spokesperson said in a statement.

"The driver was combative with law enforcement, but was quickly placed under arrest," it said. "Around the same time, a second individual jumped a barricade near the northwest corner of Lafayette Park. That individual was also quickly placed under arrest."

Secret Service said both incidents were under investigation.

It was not clear if the two were related.

items.title: Pentagon chief Hegseth expected to face House impeachment vote this week
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 9 (Reuters) - Pete Hegseth, the US defense secretary, calls himself the secretary of war, part of his effort to rebrand a military he said was too weak and "woke" when he took office last year. Now, with an expected House impeachment vote this week, he could soon share something in common with an actual secretary of war.

William Belknap, who held that title in 1876, became the first, and to date only, civilian leader of the US military to be impeached by Congress.

US Representative Thomas Massie, a Kentucky Republican, introduced eight articles of impeachment on Monday, setting off a two-day clock for a potential House vote on charges including waging war against Iran without congressional approval and other abuses of power.

Massie, addressing reporters, cautioned that Republican leadership could try to avoid a straight vote on impeachment by trying to dismiss it with a procedural motion.

"They may try to get out of an actual vote on the substance of this. We should have a vote and a rigorous debate on these eight articles of impeachment," he told a press conference.

Congressional sources say the resolution may have the votes to pass even with President Donald Trump's Republicans still controlling the House until Democrats take over on January 3. Conviction appears unlikely in the Senate, however, where a two-thirds majority is required and Republicans hold 53 of 100 seats.

President Donald Trump, in an interview with Reuters on Monday, strongly defended Hegseth, pointing to the US military's performance in Iran and Venezuela: "Well, he won two wars. I don't know how you can impeach him." He later told a White House press conference he would stand by Hegseth even if he is impeached, and called Massie a "stone-cold loser."

House Speaker Mike Johnson opposed the effort, saying impeachment "in the middle of hostilities abroad" would be "a terrible thing for our allies and our enemies to see."

Voter anger over the war helped Democrats win control of Congress in last week's midterm elections, intensifying Republican divisions over a conflict that Vice President JD Vance has publicly questioned and Hegseth has defended as "courageous and historic."

Accused of taking huge kickbacks, Belknap handed President Ulysses Grant his resignation ahead of his scheduled impeachment vote and, according to a Senate history, "burst into tears." The House impeached him anyway, but the Senate later acquitted him after falling short of the required two-thirds majority.

By contrast, Hegseth is promising to stay and fight.

HEGSETH SAYS HE IS NOT WORRIED

Hegseth has mounted a social media campaign, saying in a defiant video message last week that he would not back down. He also drew a comparison to Trump, who was impeached twice, saying: "It didn't work against President Trump, and it won't work with me."

Asked if he had enough Republican support to defeat the impeachment push, Hegseth said on Monday: "We're not worried about that." He announced a Tuesday press conference, his first at the Pentagon since May.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who is also White House national security adviser, called the impeachment push "unfair," telling reporters: "I think Pete's done a good job. I really do."

Trump, speaking with Reuters, extolled Hegseth's performance in the Iran war, which is at an impasse, and with Venezuela, where the US military deposed that country's president, Nicolás Maduro, in a surprise January commando raid on his compound in the Venezuelan capital.

"Well, what about impeaching the people from Vietnam, Afghanistan, Iraq and all of that, where we fought forever and nothing happened?" Trump asked.

DEFENSE SPENDING AT RISK?

Some Republican lawmakers have expressed concern that if Hegseth stays, his strained relationship with Congress will undermine the Trump administration's push for a $1.5 trillion defense spending package.

Massie, a Trump critic who is leaving office in January, warned in a statement on Monday that impeachment would be "much gentler" than what's in store for Hegseth once Democrats take control in January.

"They will hold hearings and trials. President Trump should replace Secretary Hegseth now while he can still get a replacement confirmed in the Senate," Massie said.

Democrats have promised to investigate Hegseth over issues including the firing of the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff and other senior leaders.

House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries said on Sunday he was a "hard yes" on a measure to impeach Hegseth.

US Senator Chuck Schumer, a New York Democrat who is expected to become majority leader, said on Monday the Senate needs to put Hegseth on trial.

"Hegseth waged this war illegally, in open defiance of the Constitution and multiple War Powers Resolutions this Congress passed to end the fighting," he said.

Massie's articles of impeachment accuse Hegseth of "high crimes and misdemeanors" ranging from waging the Iran war to various alleged abuses of power, including violating the free speech rights of US Senator Mark Kelly, an Arizona Democrat.

Last year, Hegseth sought to prosecute Kelly after he and five other Democrats in Congress with backgrounds in the military and intelligence urged US troops to refuse illegal orders. Hegseth accused them of sedition, something Trump at the time said in a social media post was "punishable by DEATH!"

Reporting by Phil Stewart and Patricia Zengerle; additional reporting by Steve Holland and David Morgan; editing by Don Durfee and Howard Goller

items.title: At a Jackson store, high prices show why Mississippi US Senate race is so close
items.content_html:
JACKSON, Mississippi, Nov 9 (Reuters) - Maria Lopez sees the customers at the Mississippi grocery store she manages struggle to afford the basics. It's not much easier for her: she keeps the heater off in her car to save gas and even buying milk at her own store can be hard.

"Instead of getting a big gallon, we'll do half a gallon," Lopez, a 42-year-old whose store is in Jackson, said, adding that she is also struggling to afford health insurance and prescriptions. "It's just me and my daughter... I don't know how other families are making it happen that don't have food stamps."

Lopez's experience is a window into one of the issues that drove this month's midterm election wins for Democrats, as American voters turned on President Donald Trump. Democrats picked up at least 41 seats in the House of Representatives and at least 7 in the Senate, with votes still being counted in a close Mississippi race that could send the state's first Democrat to the US Senate in 44 years.

Mississippi is the second-poorest US state, trailing only Louisiana. In the capital city of Jackson, over a quarter of its 141,000 residents live in poverty, more than double the US average, according to the Census Bureau.

That made prices – of gas, of food, of almost everything – a key issue in this year's midterm elections in Mississippi where Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith was accused by Democrats of being insensitive when she told voters worried about the price of beef that they should pick another protein. Democrat Scott Colom made the most of her misstep, suggesting in a campaign ad that the state "pick another senator" instead.

Hinds County, which includes Jackson, has long been one of Mississippi's most reliable Democratic strongholds.

This year, 80% of voters in the county backed Colom and 19% supported Hyde-Smith. Republicans' share of the vote in Hinds County fell by more than 7 percentage points from the 2024 election that returned Trump to the White House, according to Reuters and USA Today.

COULD EXTEND DEMOCRATS' MAJORITY

The outcome in Mississippi and Alaska, where the Senate race is also not yet called, will determine whether the Democratic Party extends its sweeping election victory.

For Lopez, who supports Colom, the election was less about party politics than the hope that whoever wins can ease the burden on household budgets.

At the independent Dash Food Market, which serves many low-income shoppers, she sees the strain every day.

"I used to get like six bags or seven bags," Tonya Plunkett, 50, a retired state worker who supports Colom, said of a $60 grocery trip. "Now $60 of groceries give me one bag, and you've got to decide what's important: medicine or food or gas."

Nesha Thomas, a fast-food employee and mother of six, said stretching a paycheck has become increasingly difficult. She cast her vote for Colom.

"I spend every dime that I get on my kids, so therefore I'm always broke," she said. "Scott is trying to help us bring these prices down, especially gas prices because they are outrageous."

The squeeze is also hitting Dash, where sales are down sharply from a year ago, according to Lopez. On a recent Friday, sales were about half their normal level, she said.

That worries her not only because she needs the job at Dash, but because it is one of the few grocery stores in the neighborhood.

"The community needs the store," Lopez said. "I need my job."

items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 9 (Reuters) - US Assistant Attorney General Brett Shumate, head of the Justice Department's civil division, has resigned, Attorney General Todd Blanche announced on Monday in a post on X.

Shumate is the fourth senior Justice Department official to resign since President Donald Trump's Republicans suffered significant losses in the midterm elections last week. Here's what to know about his tenure:

  • Shumate, who also served in the Justice Department in Trump's first term, oversaw a division that challenged corporate diversity initiatives, healthcare clinics that served transgender minors and local governments that did not cooperate with the Trump administration's immigration crackdown.
  • Shumate also defended Trump's efforts to revoke citizenship from naturalized immigrants in court.
  • Like other divisions in DOJ, the Civil Division has lost significant staff since Trump won reelection two years ago, including in the unit that defends Trump's policies in court. Under Shumate, the division recently offered signing bonuses of up to $25,000.
  • It was not immediately clear why Shumate was resigning. Other senior DOJ officials who have recently left include Harmeet Dhillon, who led the Civil Rights Division; John Eisenberg, who headed the National Security Division; and Jason Reding Quiñones, a US attorney who pursued probes into past criminal investigations of Trump.

items.title: 'Trump has cost us': After midterm losses, MAGA asks if it's over
items.content_html:
DALLAS, Nov 8 (Reuters) - As Republicans faced a nationwide drubbing in Tuesday's midterm elections, supporters streamed out of a Dallas ballroom where they'd hoped to toast a win for US Senate candidate Ken Paxton, a favorite of President Donald Trump.

In the hotel bar, Michael Little, a 59-year-old businessman and three-time Trump voter, stared at the president's image on a television screen. "People are pissed off at Trump. Trump has cost us," he said, capturing a sentiment rippling through the president's Make America Great Again movement after the Republican Party's worst electoral defeat in decades.

Across the coalition, some supporters who once viewed Trump as MAGA's greatest asset are beginning to question whether he's become its biggest liability.

The midterm losses amounted to more than a repudiation of Trump. They were a referendum on the political and cultural movement he built. A defining force in American politics that began as a campaign slogan during Trump's 2016 presidential run now faces a potentially existential reckoning after voters disillusioned with soaring fuel prices, the Iran war and Washington corruption delivered Democrats decisive congressional majorities.

Trump's first major response to the midterms came on Friday. Instead of changing course, he doubled down on the movement's core. He promoted Stephen Miller, the main architect of the administration's hardline immigration crackdown, to chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles. Wiles was seen as a stabilizing force inside an often chaotic White House.

The move was celebrated by some of MAGA's most ardent influencers, who saw it as a return to the anti-immigration agenda at the movement's roots. "Exactly the energy we need," right-wing influencer Benny Johnson posted on X to his 4.1 million followers. "Solid move. It's Miller Time."

The White House did not directly answer Reuters' questions about why Republicans lost, the defeat of candidates who embraced Trump's false 2020 election claims, or where MAGA goes from here. Instead, it pointed to Trump's remarks on Wednesday, when he said, "If I were on the ballot, we would have won." He also said it was "largely true" that the Iran war had cost Republicans because "it drove the gasoline up," but that he'd do it again.

For nearly a decade, MAGA has reshaped the Republican Party and transformed national debates on issues such as trade, immigration, race and gender. The movement installed loyalists throughout federal agencies, cracked down on immigration and pressured corporations and public institutions to retreat from diversity, equity and inclusion initiatives. MAGA survived the fallout from the January 6, 2021, attack on the US Capitol and propelled Trump back to the White House. In Trump's second term, MAGA was no longer a faction of the Republican Party; it was the party.

Now, the Democrats' sweeping victory has forced the movement to grapple with an unexpected question: Is MAGA over?

Reuters interviews with more than a dozen MAGA activists, influencers, party strategists, Christian nationalist leaders and researchers who track right-wing politics, along with a review of MAGA supporters' posts and podcasts since Tuesday, show a movement turning its anger on itself.

The stolen-election claims that have driven MAGA since Democrat Joe Biden beat Trump in the 2020 presidential election have mostly gone quiet. Instead, supporters are blaming Republican leaders and Trump's advisers, and in some cases the president himself, for broken promises on living costs, the Iran war and the government's decision to redact or withhold major portions of its investigative files on late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

MAGA's factions also disagree about what comes next. Some want a return to populist and nationalist basics. Some want a movement less tied to one man. And a vocal minority say MAGA is already dead.

"We have to rebuild," Steve Bannon, a prominent MAGA proponent, podcaster and former Trump White House adviser, told Reuters. He urged the party to double down on an aggressive populist and nationalist agenda and praised Trump for elevating Miller. "Miller's appointment as chief of staff underpins my point," he said. "There is no more hardcore MAGA proponent than Stephen."

As pro-Trump internet forums digested the election results, a notable slice of self-described MAGA loyalists – more than 20% – raised doubts about the movement's leadership and direction, according to an analysis of social media traffic done for Reuters by PeakMetrics, a data intelligence firm. About half of that cohort remained supportive of the MAGA movement but no longer backed Trump as its leader. The other half remained loyal to, though critical of, the president himself.

The analysis was based on 12,850 posts sampled from a universe of 4.6 million Trump-related comments on X and Reddit from 9 p.m. on Election Day to 8 p.m. the next evening. It found broad concern among MAGA supporters as the results became clear. Of the posts that assigned blame for the rout, nearly a third said concerns about the Iran war and Israel's influence over US policy had overshadowed Trump's message. A quarter said Republicans not fully committed to the MAGA agenda had undermined the movement.

The results left Trump facing large Democratic majorities in both chambers of Congress. Democrats could hold as many as 56 of the Senate's 100 seats, more than enough to block his judicial nominees. They will also hold governorships in all seven battleground states Trump won in 2024, and they swept every statewide race in Texas, which last backed a Democrat for president in 1976.

Some prominent Republicans, long wary of a MAGA base that punished dissent, have begun openly criticizing Trump.

Republican US Senator Ron Johnson of Wisconsin said on Saturday that corruption was present in "all branches of government," including "I'm sad to say, within the Trump administration." He cited Calley Means, a former White House adviser who told "The Joe Rogan Experience" podcast on Friday that Trump's top aides catered to special interests and blocked policies popular with Trump's Make America Healthy Again movement. Voters "were expecting us to drain the swamp, but it seems like the swamp won," Johnson told Fox News.

Asked about Johnson's remarks and Means' accusations, White House spokesperson Allison Schuster did not address the corruption allegations, saying Trump had "made incredible strides to Make America Healthy Again."

On Sunday, Republican US Representative Marlin Stutzman of Indiana, who won reelection despite his party's losses, called Trump's promotion of Miller a "bad mistake." "You don't promote those who were in charge," Stutzman told CNN. "He's not liked out here in the Midwest by people. They don't like his tone," he said of Miller.

White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said Miller had "been a key player" in delivering on Trump's agenda "since day one" and would "continue to deliver historic successes" as chief of staff. The White House also pointed to statements from 19 Republican lawmakers supporting Miller's promotion.

'MAGA IS STALE'

The midterm losses have muffled one of MAGA's loudest refrains: Since Tuesday, talk of election fraud has virtually vanished among right-wing influencers.

"I have been banging the drum of rigged and stolen elections since 2020, but that is not why we lost the midterms," Rogan O'Handley, a MAGA influencer who posts under the name DC_Draino, wrote on X to his 2.3 million followers. "We lost because we failed to fix the things voters sent us to do." He didn't respond to a request for comment.

After the 2020 election, Trump supporter Isabella DeLuca was among thousands who stormed the US Capitol on January 6, 2021. She was charged with five crimes, including theft of a table from inside the Capitol, and pleaded not guilty. Her case was dismissed after Trump returned to office and pardoned her.

This time, the 26-year-old conservative influencer directed her anger toward what she described as out-of-touch Republican leaders who failed to appeal to Gen Z voters on affordability, avoiding foreign wars and other key issues.

"Republicans were just lazy. They felt like that they were entitled to people's votes and that people would vote for them no matter what," DeLuca told Reuters. "It goes to show you that you do have to earn people's votes, and that even in a super red state like Texas, you're not untouchable."

The MAGA movement this year appeared "tired," she said.

That sentiment was echoed in online right-wing forums, said Jennifer Golbeck, a University of Maryland professor who has analyzed MAGA-related posts since 2016. She said engagement by Trump's most loyal backers has steadily declined since January, including a 27% drop in posts and comments on Patriots.Win, a popular MAGA forum.

"The enthusiasm and the passion even among this hardest core group of supporters hasn't really been there," Golbeck said. "They are saying that 'MAGA is stale.' It's not new and exciting like it once was."

Fox News, a cable network that has long been a key platform for MAGA voices, saw a sharp decline in viewership ahead of the midterms, with its total daytime audience down 27% in October from a year earlier, according to Nielsen, the audience measurement firm. In a statement to Reuters, Fox said it drew more viewers than its cable-news rivals on election night. "FOX News has been the number one network in cable news for a quarter century," the network said.

Some prominent right-wing influencers blamed the president's advisers or Republican lawmakers – but rarely Trump himself – for ignoring key voter concerns. In posts, online broadcasts and interviews with Reuters, many blamed dissatisfaction with the economy, though they differed on other reasons for Tuesday's results.

It wasn't just failure to address affordability that "crushed" Republicans, said Ben Shapiro, co-founder of the conservative site Daily Wire, on his online show on Wednesday. "If you're talking about an electoral catastrophe – a wipeout like we saw last night – you need more ingredients. Here are the other ingredients: chaos and corruption."

Laura Loomer, an influencer close to Trump, wrote on X: "America is over and the American Dream is dead." Yet she told Reuters the losses did not signal the end of MAGA, arguing that anyone seeking the 2028 Republican presidential nomination would need Trump's base.

"The Republican Party belongs to President Trump," Loomer said. "The MAGA movement is still the majority of the GOP base, and whoever wants to run for president in 2028 on the GOP ticket, they would be unwise to be dismissive of President Trump."

On Thursday, Loomer put her podcast on hiatus, saying she had been "running on empty for too long" and needed to focus on her personal life and upcoming wedding. She'll return in January, she added.

BROKEN PROMISES

The midterms also tested the beliefs that have held MAGA together, and some of them are giving way.

The Democratic sweep dealt a significant setback to the election denial movement, a central pillar of MAGA politics since Trump's 2020 defeat. Candidates who embraced his false claims of widespread voter fraud lost heavily, including several who had worked to overturn the 2020 result. Election deniers will hold at least 41 fewer congressional and statewide offices next year, and they have lost 70% of the called races for statewide posts that oversee elections, according to States United Action, a nonprofit that tracks such candidates. Trump made no effort to contest the results and instead blamed Republicans for the defeat.

With few close races and no credible basis for a challenge, many prominent pro-Trump election skeptics dropped fraud allegations and urged supporters to keep organizing. A handful of allies still alleged, without evidence, that the vote was rigged. Mike Lindell, the MyPillow founder and promoter of false claims that machines flipped votes in 2020, said he was not concerned by Trump's pledge to accept the results. "That's his opinion. I've got a different opinion," Lindell told Reuters. "I think it's all been stolen."

But such claims stayed largely on the fringe, even among Republicans. Without contested races, the MAGA election denial movement risks losing the money, attention and momentum that sustained it. "Nobody's going to be putting money behind it," said Wendy Via, co-founder of the Global Project Against Hate and Extremism, a nonprofit that tracks hate speech and extremism.

Retired Lieutenant General Mike Flynn, who falsely claimed the 2020 election was stolen and is a popular figure in the Christian nationalist wing of the MAGA movement, accepted the defeat. He called the results "a massacre" and criticized Trump and his administration for failing to deliver on pledges ranging from lowering costs to releasing the government's investigative files on Epstein.

Responding to Vice President JD Vance's assessment on X that the Iran war was "the reason we lost," Flynn wrote: "the sheer number of broken promises is why the blue tsunami happened."

Flynn also criticized Christian voters for failing to show up. "As a Catholic and a Christian, I'm sorely embarrassed and disappointed," he wrote.

Other prominent Christian nationalists were divided over whether MAGA can outlast Trump.

Douglas Wilson, a Christian nationalist pastor who was invited by US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to deliver a sermon at the Pentagon in February, told Reuters that MAGA "is not going anywhere" but must become less personality-driven and more focused on border control, tax cuts and avoiding foreign wars.

Joel Webbon, a far-right Christian nationalist pastor from Texas, was far less sanguine. "Trump lost this all by himself," he said in a video on X, arguing that the president abandoned his base by embracing Israel, launching the war in Iran and failing to follow through on releasing the Epstein files and mass deportations.

"MAGA is dead," Webbon wrote in an accompanying post. "Forever."

items.title: EXCLUSIVE: Rubio warns top staff against conflicts of interest as Republicans look to 2028
items.content_html:
• Rubio warns unethical behavior will bring firing regardless of official's connections, one source says
  • State requires Rubio office approval for all political travel, sources say
  • Warning followed Kimberly Guilfoyle's exit after reports she sold access for favors

WASHINGTON, Nov 7 (Reuters) - US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has moved to tighten control over the State Department, telling senior officials that staff must stay in their lanes and avoid actions that present conflicts of interest, four people familiar with the matter said.

Rubio's message, delivered in a meeting last week before the Republican Party's electoral losses on Tuesday, comes as its leading figures attempt to put distance between themselves and an increasingly unpopular Trump administration.

The meeting followed the high-profile resignation of US Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle in mid-October after news reports raised concerns that she sold access to Trump administration officials in exchange for money, gifts and favors.

Guilfoyle has called the reports false and in a post on social media said she would defend her reputation.

Rubio told the meeting, which included many of the roughly two dozen assistant secretaries of state, that unethical behavior would result in a firing, regardless of how well-connected an official might be, said one of the people.

He added that too many officials were making decisions or pushing policy agendas without coordinating and that significant decisions required his signoff or that of Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau, according to the people, who spoke on the condition of anonymity. Details of the meeting have not previously been reported.

The State Department declined to comment on the meeting.

Soon after the meeting, three of the people said, the State Department's policy chief, Jeremy Lewin, was forced out of his job in part due to concerns that he was working on matters outside his area without proper coordination. The exact details of those concerns remain unclear.

None of the people who spoke to Reuters suggested Lewin's departure was linked to any incidents of ethical misconduct. Lewin joined the government as part of Elon Musk's Department of Government Efficiency and helped dismantle the US Agency for International Development, which oversaw US foreign assistance.

Rubio and others within the State Department leadership were frustrated with his "freelancing" and going against "certain directives from the Secretary," one of the people said, without providing specific examples.

Lewin, who was appointed to his senior role just over two months ago, said on social media last month that he had stepped down from his role to return to the private sector.

Asked for comment, a State Department official said: "It was mutually agreed it was time (for Lewin) to move on."

Lewin said in a statement to Reuters that his departure was planned several weeks before it was announced and he denied he was fired.

"The suggestion that I was fired is false. As planned for weeks with the Secretary and his team, after staying longer than expected to finish key projects, I resigned my position prior to the midterms to assume a private sector role and plan my wedding," he said.

"It had nothing to do with any meeting or policy regarding the management of the department."

Rubio's frustrations also included excessive overseas travel by political staff, which has led to a requirement that Rubio's office approve all political travel, according to another one of the people.

REPUBLICANS LOOK BEYOND MIDTERM LOSSES

The 2028 presidential race began shifting into gear almost immediately after Tuesday's midterm elections delivered control of Congress to the Democrats. Vice President JD Vance and Republican Senator Ted Cruz offered post-mortems on X that many strategists saw as political vision statements as the campaign season begins.

Rubio himself has sought to play down reports that he is considering a run, but he has also not publicly ruled it out. If he does, his management of the State Department could emerge as a topic of conversation on the campaign trail.

President Donald Trump's administration has faced consistent accusations of self-dealing and Democrats have said they will put dealings between Trump aides and foreign officials under the microscope when they take control of Congress in January and begin launching official investigations.

The Trump administration has denied allegations of self-dealing.

Shortly after Guilfoyle left the administration in October, Rubio sent a department-wide memo reminding diplomats to "avoid conflicts of interest," according to multiple media outlets.

He subsequently denied that the memo was sent as a result of Guilfoyle's departure, telling reporters that he had in fact meant to send it weeks earlier, but that it had been held up for bureaucratic reasons.

Like other parts of the Trump administration, Rubio's department has lost officials recently.

In October, US Special Representative for Global Partnerships Paolo Zampolli was fired after Politico reported an email thread between him and Landau, in which Landau accused Zampolli of working outside his "lane" of cultural diplomacy, saying Zampolli kept wanting to work on issues outside his remit in contravention of Landau's orders.

Reuters could not determine what those issues were.

Shortly after his departure, Zampolli wrote on X that special envoy appointments last one year by statute and that Trump had extended his appointment by more than six months.

Reporting by Gram Slattery, Humeyra Pamuk and Jonathan Landay; Editing by Don Durfee and Sanjeev Miglani

items.title: After midterm rout, Vance tries to build his own 2028 brand
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 7 (Reuters) - Late in his blitz to salvage Republicans' midterm fortunes, Vice President JD Vance shifted strategy. He talked less about President Donald Trump and more about the issues that define his own political identity.

Vance argued the case for Republicans, who lost control of Congress in Tuesday's vote, almost exclusively through the lens of his policy portfolio, according to a Reuters review of half a dozen speeches since the Republican convention in September.

He bypassed Trump's signature policies including the Iran war and deportations as polls showed the president's sagging popularity dragging down Republican office-seekers.

The change was deliberate, according to two people familiar with the strategy. Vance and his advisers saw the issues he championed — economic nationalism, foreign policy restraint, and public safety — as politically potent subjects he could address with authority. While Trump embraced them as part of his MAGA movement, Vance had emerged as their lead crusader, the people said.

The shift offered an early glimpse of how the 42-year-old vice president could chart his own course as Republicans begin looking beyond Trump.

Vance hasn't said whether he will run for president in 2028, and Trump hasn't endorsed him or anyone else. But Vance is viewed as a leading potential contender who some Republican officials say will need to inherit much of Trump's coalition while separating himself from his boss's baggage.

Vance took a more public step on Wednesday toward reinforcing his own political brand with an unusually blunt election postmortem. In a social media post, he blamed the Iran war for Republicans' midterm defeat and laid out a platform for a Republican rebound.

He called for a swift end to the conflict and urged Republicans to focus on affordability, reevaluate foreign relations and overhaul the US relationship with Israel.

Trump has called Americans' affordability concerns a Democratic "hoax." He launched a war against Iran following sustained lobbying from Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Trump went on to endorse Netanyahu in the Israeli election.

VANCE MAKES UNEASE AT THE WAR PUBLIC

The post for the first time put Vance openly on the side of ending the war.

Three people familiar with the White House and Vance's communications told Reuters that the vice president was not breaking with Trump and said White House chief of staff Susie Wiles knew in advance about Vance's post.

On Friday, Trump reshuffled senior White House leadership, replacing Wiles with Stephen Miller in a move that suggests the White House plans to double down on some of Trump's more hardline policies.

Trump has acknowledged the Iran war played a role in the Republican rout because of the resulting high gas prices but has continued to defend it. "I would have done nothing different," he told reporters on Wednesday.

Reuters could not determine whether Trump was aware of the post in advance.

Donald Trump Jr., the president's eldest son, endorsed Vance's remarks on social media, along with some conservative allies.

The dialogue further elevated Vance as a potential post-Trump conservative standard-bearer, said Michael Ricci, a Republican strategist and former adviser to House Speakers John Boehner and Paul Ryan.

USING THE MEGAPHONE OF THE VICE PRESIDENCY

He said Vance's message forced conservatives to debate the merits of the war, and more broadly, what core tenets Republican presidential candidates should embrace in 2028.

"It's simplistic to say this about him looking for ways to differentiate himself from Trump," Ricci said. "This is about him using his megaphone of the vice presidency to set the terms of debate."

Representatives for Vance declined to comment. White House representatives referred Reuters to Trump's comments on Wednesday, when he told reporters he understood Vance's perspective on the election results.

Democrats are poised to tie Vance – or any Republican nominee – to Trump in 2028, especially if Trump plays a large role in vetting conservative hopefuls.

"There's a real challenge of how you position yourself to be viable in a general election while winning a primary that still requires you to bow down and kiss the ring," said Igor Volsky, a Democratic strategist.

Vance's brand did not emerge from the midterms unscathed. Republicans lost in states where he campaigned. Some of the strategies he endorsed – including an ad by Ohio gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy that cast doubt on the sexual abuse suffered by the victorious Democratic candidate, Amy Acton – may have swung races away from Republicans.

Other possible 2028 presidential contenders have offered their diagnoses of the midterm defeat. US Senator Ted Cruz of Texas said Republicans hadn't done enough on affordability. Florida Governor Ron DeSantis said losing candidates had focused too heavily on transgender issues and neglected voter concerns about data centers and artificial intelligence. Secretary of State Marco Rubio has stayed silent.

Vance's effort to shape the debate was visible during the closing days of the campaign.

In stump speeches, he told voters to support Republicans because they would investigate fraud in federal health care and antipoverty programs, tying that to the White House's immigration agenda and cost of living. He almost entirely ignored the Iran war and gas prices, and seldom mentioned Trump by name.

"I want my kids to raise a family in a country that is vibrant and thriving and free and prosperous. I want the simple things," Vance told one of his final rallies in North Carolina. "And because I want that for me, I want it for you too."
