items.title: Four things to note from Friday's US jobs report
items.content_html:
Nov 6 (Reuters) - The US economy added 165,000 jobs in October — 100,000 more than expected by economists — and the unemployment rate ticked down unexpectedly to 4.1% amid a fairly broad-based improvement in the job market.

Here is a look at four notable data points from the Bureau of Labor Statistics report.

  • Foreign-born workers account for all net labor force participation and employment gains since July
  • Manufacturing adds 101,000 jobs since December 2025, leaving net gain of 8,000 under Trump
  • Median and average unemployment spells are longest in about a decade excluding the pandemic
  • Information and finance remain weakest in AI-exposed industries

FOREIGN-BORN WORKERS LEAD GAINS

The US labor force had contracted notably during President Donald Trump's first year back in office, and economists connected the large outflows of foreign-born workers that led the decline to Trump's immigration crackdown. Recently that has been reversing.

The workforce has expanded sharply in the last three months in particular, and all of the net gains in labor force participation and employment -- as measured by the payrolls report's household survey -- have come from foreign-born workers. Employment and participation among native-born workers have fallen since July.

MANUFACTURING COMEBACK

Factory work is another corner of the job market experiencing a U-turn to the upside. In Trump's first year, the manufacturing sector shed 93,000 jobs even as he imposed tariffs on imported goods to try to boost domestic factory employment.

That decline began reversing this year, and since December 2025 the sector has added 101,000 jobs, leading to a net gain of 8,000 factory jobs since Trump returned to the White House.

JOBLESS FOR LONGER

The recent uptick in the pace of hiring has not yet begun to shorten the length of time that people who lose a job are out of work. While layoffs remain subdued and job gains have been sufficient in number to lower the unemployment rate, those with the misfortune of losing a job on average are remaining out of work for longer than any time in the past five years.

Excluding the short-lived surge in unemployment during the COVID-19 pandemic, both the median and average duration of unemployment -- 11.9 weeks and 27.1 weeks, respectively -- are the longest in about a decade.

AI IMPACTS

Most economists agree that the ever-widening adoption of artificial intelligence tools by employers has yet to produce major job displacements across the economy. That doesn't mean they are entirely absent.

"The most AI-exposed sectors, information and finance, continued to struggle and have shed jobs on a trend basis," Michael Pearce, chief US economist at Oxford Economics, noted following the jobs report. "By contrast, professional and business services, which also has high AI adoption, bucked that trend and added 70,000 jobs in October while seeing upward revisions to past months. Those gains were broad, spanning temporary help and management and technical consulting services."

Reporting by Dan Burns; Editing by Andrea Ricci

items.title: Trump makes hardliner Stephen Miller his chief of staff after midterm defeat
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 6 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump named longtime aide Stephen Miller as his chief of staff on Friday, giving the architect of some of his toughest domestic policies one of the most powerful jobs in Washington after Republicans lost control of Congress.

Miller, who will replace Susie Wiles, assumes the role as the president prepares to confront a Democratic-led House of Representatives and Senate and a wave of congressional investigations into his administration.

A longtime proponent of expansive presidential authority, Miller takes over at a moment when the Republican Party's defeat in Tuesday's midterm elections could leave Trump more reliant on executive power to advance his domestic agenda.

In a social media post, Trump called Miller "one of my most trusted advisors," and praised Wiles for doing "an outstanding job." Trump said the change would take effect on Monday.

A White House official said Miller's appointment signals that Trump has no intention of rethinking his policies and instead is rewarding his most loyal aides.

"He's not changing course," the official said, despite tens of millions of American voters repudiating Trump's domestic agenda and foreign policy.

Trump said this week he was willing to work with Democrats on Capitol Hill. But elevating Miller, who is known for being caustic and uncompromising, could signal a more confrontational approach and a renewed push to advance the president's agenda on immigration and other issues, several White House officials said.

Trump had been displeased with his political and communications operations in the run-up to Tuesday's election as his public approval ratings fell near record lows. This week, he said the White House needed to be "more aggressive" as Democrats retake congressional power, according to a person briefed on the matter.

"The mission now is more clear than ever," Miller said on X after his appointment. "Fight with all of our soul to support our President and defend this magnificent Republic."

Hakeem Jeffries, who is set to become the new Democratic speaker of the House, responded to the announcement by calling Miller a "reckless extremist" in a posting on X.

MILLER DRIVING IMMIGRATION CRACKDOWN

Miller, 41, is one of Trump's longest-serving aides and one of only a few who served throughout his first and second terms in office.

Since Trump's return to the White House in 2025, Miller has officially served as deputy chief of staff under Wiles, but he has wielded outsize influence across much of Trump's domestic agenda and has had the president's ear.

He is perhaps best known for driving Trump's aggressive immigration crackdown, setting a goal of 3,000 arrests a day. The efforts to meet that target pushed masked US immigration officers into communities around the country, increasingly arresting people with no criminal records and who had been living in the country for decades.

The crackdown, however, gets poor marks with Americans. Just 36% of respondents to a Reuters/Ipsos poll completed early this week approve of it, with 54% disapproving.

Representative Robert Garcia, the top Democrat on the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform, said the party planned to investigate Miller's immigration policies. "Stephen Miller should lawyer up," he said.

Miller was also deeply involved in Trump's campaign to remake the federal bureaucracy, which led to the dismissal of tens of thousands of civil servants in 2025. He was also a driving force behind the administration's battles with universities, diversity programs and other institutions.

HAWKISH FOREIGN POLICY

On foreign policy, Miller has been a vocal supporter of Trump's deadly military strikes on boats suspected of carrying drugs in the Caribbean and Pacific, a campaign that has raised legal questions.

He has also praised US and Israeli strikes in Iran and defended a naval blockade and sanctions as ways to weaken Tehran and curb its ability to threaten its neighbors. It is not clear whether that is still his view after voters punished Republicans this week in part for the economic fallout from the Iran war.

Marc Short, who was chief of staff to then-Vice President Mike Pence in Trump's first term, said that in Miller, Trump is "getting someone who is wed to him" and who is willing to battle Congress over issues like immigration and congressional investigations.

"It would not suggest that there is high expectation for bipartisan legislation," Short said in an interview.

Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, who faces Democratic calls for impeachment over the Iran war, celebrated Miller's promotion with a social media post reading, "Patriots in control," reflecting the enthusiasm of some Trump allies for putting Miller in a position of greater authority.

SHAKE UP AFTER ELECTION SETBACK

The chief of staff typically wields great influence as the president's gatekeeper. The person manages White House staff, organizes the president's time and schedule, and oversees other government departments and lawmakers.

Wiles, 69, who submitted her resignation on Thursday night, will move to Trump's political operation, according to a White House official.

The veteran political operative from Florida was the first woman to serve as White House chief of staff.

She brought decades of political experience to the role and was regarded as running a more disciplined operation than some of Trump's prior top aides. She maintained her role even while undergoing treatment earlier this year for early-stage breast cancer.

Wiles rarely challenged Trump's policies but brought discipline to an often chaotic operation and was seen as a voice of reason. Her exit raises questions about who will play her role.

Trump ran through four chiefs of staff – an unusually high number – during his 2017-2021 term, as they were seen to have struggled to rein in the unpredictable president.

Reporting by Bo Erickson, Nandita Bose, Steve Holland, Jacob Bogage in Washington; Additional reporting by Bhargav Acharya and Susan Heavey; Writing by Trevor Hunnicutt; editing by Scott Malone, Colleen Jenkins, Ross Colvin and Jonathan Spicer

items.title: Democratic victories bring historic breakthroughs for women and minorities
items.content_html:
CHICAGO, Nov 4 (Reuters) - Voters across the US elected a historic slate of women, candidates of color and other underrepresented politicians on Tuesday, reshaping the face of political leadership as Democrats rode a wave of dissatisfaction with President Donald Trump's administration to major gains nationwide.

Democrats flipped control of both the House of Representatives and Senate while winning key statewide races, delivering a series of milestone victories.

Gina Hinojosa became the first Latina elected governor of Texas, Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan the first Muslim elected to the US Senate and Deb Haaland of New Mexico the first Native American woman elected governor. In Georgia, Keisha Lance Bottoms became the first Black woman elected governor of a US state while Xavier Becerra was the first Latino elected as governor of California. Chris Pappas of New Hampshire made history as the first openly gay man elected to the US Senate.

The breakthroughs marked a striking expansion of who holds political power at the highest levels of American government, in a country where people of marginalized backgrounds have long been underrepresented.

"From coast to coast, voters ... spoke with clarity. Democrats must now govern courageously," former Georgia gubernatorial candidate Stacey Abrams said in a statement.

Pollsters and political analysts said the Democratic gains appeared to stem from a combination of economic frustration and dissatisfaction with the Iran war, tariffs, aggressive immigration enforcement, perceived government corruption and the country's broader direction, among other issues.

Democrats made unexpected gains in deeply conservative states, suggesting the party attracted Republicans while rebuilding support within its traditional coalition, analysts, civil rights leaders and grassroots voter organizations said. Black and Latino voters had become increasingly contested constituencies in recent election cycles.

"You can't take for granted the Hispanic voters in this country, the Black voters in this country, the young voters in this country, and if we don't deliver, they can swing right back," said Democratic strategist Bakari Sellers.

Democratic victories in Republican-leaning states helped flip the House and Senate and signaled a broader voter backlash against Republican leadership, said Vanderbilt University political scientist John Geer, who studies public opinion.

"It's an old-fashioned thumping that we haven't seen in quite a while," Geer said. Republicans made a series of promises in 2024, "and almost none of them were kept. This is the public's reaction to it."

Economic concerns, including the rising costs of housing, healthcare, food and fuel, cut across racial and political lines, said Greg Lewis, executive director of Souls to the Polls, a Milwaukee-based civic engagement organization.

Lewis, who voted for Wisconsin Democrat David Crowley, the state's first Black governor-elect, said voters were frustrated with the economic pressures facing their families.

"When you start getting into people's pockets, you have a problem," Lewis said.

In Texas, Hinojosa's defeat of Governor Greg Abbott ended a 31-year Republican hold on the governor's office. Democrat James Talarico defeated Republican Ken Paxton in the US Senate race, delivering one of the night's biggest surprises in a state Trump carried comfortably in 2024.

Democrat Jon Rosenthal won a seat on the Railroad Commission of Texas, becoming the first Jewish candidate elected to statewide executive office, according to the Jewish Herald-Voice.

"We all had hope, but to see it come to fruition is breathtaking," said Joshua Arce, a Texas resident and president of Partnership With Native Americans. He said the results reflected a Republican Party that had failed to offer voters a compelling policy agenda.

The election's gains in representation were not limited to Democrats. In Florida, US Representative Byron Donalds, a Republican, became the first Black governor elected in the state's history.

Melik Abdul, a Republican strategist and Trump supporter, said the result underscored tensions between the party's criticism of diversity, equity and inclusion initiatives and the growing prominence of Black Republicans.

"Republicans spent the last year linking DEI to Black people and the idea that they were unqualified. How ironic that a Black guy ends up being the biggest win that Republicans had," Abdul said.

FROM REPRESENTATION TO INFLUENCE

But experts cautioned that electoral breakthroughs do not automatically translate into greater political influence, lasting policy changes or institutional reform.

The ability of newly elected officials to shape legislation, control congressional committee agendas, direct government spending and influence party leadership will depend on the institutions they enter, the coalitions they build and the balance of power within their parties, political experts said.

Within the Congressional Black Caucus and the Democratic Party more broadly, an influx of new lawmakers could expose generational tensions between established members who hold influential leadership and committee positions and younger lawmakers seeking a greater role in shaping the party's agenda, said Nadia Brown, director of women's and gender studies at Georgetown University.

"What I think is going to happen, what we've seen is, unfortunately, is that the older members and those in leadership will cannibalize their young, and that's what I'm really concerned about," Brown said.

Brown said longstanding barriers facing many communities, especially unemployment for Black women, are unlikely to disappear simply because more women and people of color won office.

"What was broken by a stroke of a pen cannot be fixed with another, and so it's going to take time to rebuild," Brown said.

Editing by Kat Stafford and Cynthia Osterman

items.title: Cornell faculty senate declares no confidence in university leadership
items.content_html:
NEW YORK, Nov 6 (Reuters) - Cornell University's faculty senate approved a resolution of no confidence on Friday in the administration's ability to handle what it has called a sexual assault crisis, after a former student sued the university for not protecting her from an alleged 2024 gang rape.

The resolution, which 55.6% of elected faculty senators who cast votes supported, is a condemnation of Cornell's leadership from its major legislative and advisory body, but has no concrete consequences. The tally showed 37% voted against it and 7.4% abstained, Cornell University spokesperson Rebecca Valli said.

"The Faculty Senate has no confidence in the ability of the central administration to effectively address the ongoing crisis of sexual assault at Cornell University," the resolution said.

The former student, who is identified by the pseudonym Jane Doe in court documents, alleged in her civil complaint that Cornell failed to protect her from being raped.

Her lawsuit, filed in September, has also drawn criticism of the university's handling of the case in 2024. Cornell, located in Ithaca, New York, responded that it had conducted a comprehensive investigation and imposed disciplinary measures, including expulsions.

BOARD SUPPORTS PRESIDENT

In response to the resolution, Cornell University Board Chair Anne Smalling expressed the board of trustees' support for University President Michael Kotlikoff and the administration.

"Today's Faculty Senate vote reflects the deep anger across our campus and sends a clear signal that what happened to Jane Doe is unacceptable," the statement said. "We support President Kotlikoff's commitment to taking all necessary steps to ensure students are safe on campus and working together as a community to help prevent this from happening again."

Kotlikoff has not responded to the university about the vote outcome, Valli, the university spokesperson, said. Under university procedures, the president has 30 days to respond in writing, she said.

Kotlikoff said the day before voting began on October 29 that faculty discussion and debate were "an important component of Cornell's shared governance" and that the university had taken measures including adding staff to its civil rights office, expanding sexual assault prevention education, and hiring staff focused on victim advocacy.

Cornell faculty senator Risa Lieberwitz, who co-sponsored the resolution, has said the administration failed to address the sexual assault problem in a systemic way during the more than a decade Kotlikoff has served in senior leadership. Kotlikoff has been Cornell president since March last year.

"Students, faculty, and staff have lost trust that sexual assault cases will be handled properly," Lieberwitz said in an online discussion of the resolution on the Cornell website in late October. "This will have a chilling effect on reporting, creating fear that reporting sexual assault to this administration will be ineffective and even damaging."

Dean of Faculty Chris Schaffer had previously said in a post that he opposed the resolution because it did not "articulate the specific failures underlying its judgment or the consequences it seeks."

"When we make a judgment this consequential, we should state clearly what has failed and what we expect to change," he wrote. "This resolution falls short of that standard."

In a separate post ahead of the vote, Schaffer said that passage of a no confidence resolution would result in "no binding consequence."

items.title: In Republican collapse, Colorado military town elects Democrat for the first time
items.content_html:
COLORADO SPRINGS, Colorado, Nov 6 (Reuters) - Colorado Springs, a military town and global center for Christian evangelism, has sent a Republican to Washington every election since its US House of Representatives district was created in 1970.

Then came 2026.

The victory of Jessica Killin, an Army veteran who was among dozens of Democrats who flipped a seat this week, is one of the starkest examples of how the party built its resounding win on affordability issues, demographics and candidates, one district at a time.

In an area with five military installations, where soldiers pack fast-food restaurants at lunchtime, Killin's triumph relied on votes of veterans, service members and their families, who represent about a third of the population, and for whom the war in Iran is personal. A soldier deployed from the city's Fort Carson US Army base was among the first Americans to die in the conflict.

Killin, a first-time candidate, said her win was a repudiation of Republican incumbent Jeff Crank's support for President Donald Trump and underscored voters' frustrations with the Iran war, tariffs and the Jeffrey Epstein scandal.

A supporter who canvassed for her found immigration also was on the minds of Latinos in a district where the population of metropolitan Colorado Springs more than doubled to around 782,000 in the last four decades, bringing greater ethnic diversity and a younger, more highly educated electorate.

"I am resolved to make the history that really matters, combating horrific corruption and chaos that we are all honestly sick of in Washington, DC," Killin, a former US Army paratrooper and aide to ex-second gentleman Doug Emhoff, told reporters on Thursday.

Crank had tried to portray Killin as an outsider.

"We cannot let our community turn into Denver or Boulder," Crank posted on social media last week, referring to the two Democratic-controlled cities to the north.

Killin targeted centrist and left-leaning residents in the state's second-largest city, and her hometown, who in the past three presidential cycles abandoned both major parties, swelling unaffiliated voters by nearly half to 53% of the electorate in El Paso County, according to county data.

In a metropolitan area where more than 200 space, aerospace, cybersecurity, and defense companies employ around 111,000 people, and account for over 40% of the local economy, Killin hammered Crank's support of Trump's "reckless" war in Iran and argued that Congress needed to reclaim its war-powers authority.

Karl Schneider, 57, a former US special forces officer and ex-vice chairman of the El Paso Republican Party, backed Killin to rein in a presidency he sees as militarily out of control.

"Donald Trump is a clear and present danger to the United States of America, our republic, and I think to the rest of the world," said Schneider, an executive at an AI cybersecurity advisory firm who served as a US Army Green Beret.

For Republican voter Rick Wood, 67, Crank failed to help tackle high gas and grocery prices and tied himself too closely to Trump, whose approval rating is near a career low of 32%, according to a Reuters/Ipsos national poll.

"They ran on Trump's coattails," said Wood, a US Air Force veteran.

'NEVER SEEN BEFORE'

Some Republicans interviewed by Reuters in the district that is home to the Focus on the Family evangelical organization were stunned by the blue wave, saying they feared the country would descend into communism, echoing warnings from Trump about the recent rise of left-wing Democratic candidates.

Politics professor Sara Hagedorn saw Killin, and other Democrats who won in former Republican strongholds, as a possible return to the fiscally responsible "Blue Dog" Democrats of the 1990s and early 2000s who worked across party lines.

"She has a real opportunity here to be a real moderate or independent voice within the Democratic Party," said Hagedorn, who teaches at the University of Colorado, Colorado Springs.

Killin's campaign coffers swelled after the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee listed the district as "in play" in February, the first time the committee had targeted the area.

Bruce Barron, 65, a former Republican congressional aide, canvassed for Killin in southeast Colorado Springs where the school district has around 54% Hispanic students and many of the Black community live.

"Every Hispanic I talked to, it resonates with them, the concern about Hispanics not being safe under the Trump administration," said Barron.

Killin's campaign outraised Crank's by nearly two to one with $5.6 million in funds. Crank received $5.8 million in outside spending, giving the two similar war chests.

Killin deployed over 400 volunteers to knock on over 100,000 doors while hosting around 150 events to meet voters, according to her campaign.

As Kyle Ries, 40, canvassed for Killin in south Colorado Springs, where American flags fly outside many homes and fuel-hungry pickups stand in driveways, he met conservatives willing to support Killin after they saw Crank back a war that has stoked energy prices.

"This is a candidate that this district has never seen before," Ries, an IT professional, said of Killin.

Reporting by Andrew Hay in Colorado Springs and Brad Brooks in Longmont. Editing by Donna Bryson and Alistair Bell
